Economic structure

Who holds the cards?

Who holds wealth and market power, and how scarce essentials are.

  • 6variables

21 of 31 documented or well supported

R6 · ReinforcingBargaining-power loop

Weak bargaining power and concentrated wealth reinforce each other

What it is

Who holds the money and the market

This is where the story starts: who owns what. When a small share of households holds most of the wealth and a few firms control a market, workers have less room to bargain and families have less cushion when prices rise. Housing is part of it too. Scarce homes push rents up and add to what owners already hold. These conditions decide who has spare money and time to spend on politics.

Pushes on Voice 5 and Your household 4

Pushed by Policy 3, Your household 7, Technology 1 and Outside forces 5

Inside 6 connections between its own variables

Its main loop, as a chain

Bargaining-power loop LoopR6

Reinforcing, feeds itself. When workers have less bargaining power, more of the income from production goes to owners, and wealth concentrates.

Read it aloud More workers' bargaining power, less wealth at the top, less money spent on influence, less policy tilt to insiders, and back to more workers' bargaining power.

Weakest steps L02, Plausible and L31, Plausible · One turn: over 10 years · Now running down

R15 · ReinforcingCivic-ties loop

Unions, civic ties and equal turnout reinforce each other

What it is

Who gets heard

Officials hear from people all the time, and some voices arrive louder than others. Campaign money and paid lobbying reach them directly. In many places the local reporters who once covered city hall are gone, which leaves fewer people watching. Turnout matters as well. When some groups vote far less often, officials learn whose views carry weight on election day.

Electoral competition

  • 5variables

R10 · ReinforcingSafe-seat loop

Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates

What it is

Whether voters can fire them

Accountability depends on a real chance of losing. In most districts the general election is easy to predict, so the contest that decides the seat is a low-turnout primary. Incumbents also help write the rules for their own races, from district maps to voting procedures. When few officials face a competitive race, the pressure to serve the whole electorate fades.

Pushed by Voice 4, Checks 3 and Outside forces 1

04

Governing institutions

Who checks their work?

Congress, the presidency, courts, watchdogs and the public services they run.

  • 7variables
  • 36connections
  • 11loops
  • 19reforms

21 of 36 documented or well supported

R13 · ReinforcingExecutive-power loop

Congressional weakness creates room for presidential action

What it is

Who checks power

Once in office, officials work inside a set of checks. Congress writes the laws and is supposed to oversee the executive branch. Courts settle fights over the rules, while inspectors general and agencies enforce them. When Congress lacks staff and expertise, more decisions shift to a president acting alone, and weakened watchdogs make the next shortcut easier. Most people meet all of this through public services, such as a benefit claim or a long wait on the phone.

Pushes on Voice 2, Elections 3, Policy 4, Your household 3 and Technology 4

Legitimacy

Whose side are the rules on?

Whose interests policy favors, and whether public trust follows performance.

6 of 17 documented or well supported

R1 · ReinforcingMoney-and-influence loop

Wealth and political influence reinforce each other

What it is

Whose side policy is on

Here the two questions meet. Policy can spread its benefits widely or send most of them to wealthy people and organized groups, and several studies find that the preferences of wealthier Americans get a stronger response. Trust follows what people see, and it grows when services work for them. From here the story loops back: tax breaks and rules that favor those at the top add to the wealth where it began.

What it is

What reaches your household

This layer is the kitchen-table economy: pay, prices, benefits and debts, and what is left at the end of the month. It sits under the five areas because this is where policy lands. A tax change or a new wage rule shows up here first. Strain here also flows back up, since households stretched thin have less time and money for taking part.

Technology and its effects

Who controls the machines?

Software now sits between people and many of the things they need.

What it is

The software in the middle

Software now sits between people and many of the things they need. The ranking of a social feed shapes what news people see, and pricing software helps set some rents and prices. AI is changing how work gets done and who keeps the gains. Government decides the rules these systems run under, which is why several lines here are lines of authority.

Forces from outside

Some forces push on the system from outside it. New technology, global trade, foreign interference and shocks like wars and pandemics all shift the ground under the five areas. The atlas takes them as given and tracks how the system responds to them, and who comes out ahead.

Overview

Part C · Elections · Electoral competition

In most districts, the race that decides the seat is the primary

Who picks them? Whether officials can lose their seats, and who controls the rules of elections. Accountability depends on a real chance of losing. In most districts the general election is easy to predict, so the contest that decides the seat is a low-turnout primary. Incumbents also help write the rules for their own races, from district maps to voting procedures.

Elections in numbers

  • 5variables
  • 20connections
  • 7loops run through it
  • 39problems tracked
  • 10reforms aimed here
On this page

Its five conditions

Elections holds five conditions, from safe seats to incumbents defeated

Each variable can rise or fall. The line beside it says what a higher value means, so a name such as safe seats reads as an amount.

VariableWhat it is, and why it mattersA higher value meansConnections and loops

  • VariableC1

    Seats with little electoral competition

    Districts where one party wins by a wide margin, so its candidates face little risk in the general election. The model counts seats won by more than 10 percentage points.

    In a safe seat the November winner is close to certain, so the race that matters happens earlier.

    A higher value means more seats are safe for one party.

    3 in, 2 out

    Loops: R10, R12, R4a

  • VariableC2

    How often the primary decides the winner

    The share of seats where the general election is so predictable that the primary settles who takes office. Turnout in that deciding contest can be far lower than in November.

    A small, low-turnout primary electorate ends up choosing the representative for everyone.

    A higher value means more seats are settled in the primary.

    1 in, 2 out

    Loops: R10

  • VariableC3

    The credible threat that an incumbent will lose the next election. Where seats are competitive, the threat pushes officials to respond to voters before anyone is removed.

    The chance of losing is what makes officials listen. Without it, voters lose their strongest tool.

    A higher value means incumbents face a more credible chance of defeat.

    4 in, 4 out

    Loops: B4, R10, R11, R16

  • VariableC4

    Officeholders' control over election rules

    The power of people already in office to set district maps, voting-access rules and local election choices. This is rule-setting authority, and each rule's effect needs its own evidence.

    The people who benefit from today’s maps and voting rules are often the ones who write them.

    A higher value means incumbents have more say over the rules of their own elections.

    4 in, 3 out

    Loops: R10, R12, R4a, R4b

  • VariableC5

    Incumbents defeated or pushed into retirement

    Officeholders who lose an election or retire under threat of defeat. This consequence is measured separately from the pressure they face while still in office.

    Defeats are how the system corrects itself. They show that poor performance has a cost.

    A higher value means more incumbents lose or retire under threat of defeat in an election cycle.

    1 in, 1 out

    Loops: B4

Source: Who Do They Answer To? Systems Atlas V7, snapshot October 15, 2026.

The loops that run through it

Seven loops run through Elections: six can feed themselves and one pushes back

Four loops pass through risk of losing office: R10, R11, R16 and B4. The chance of losing is what makes officials listen. Two of them meet there: R10, the safe-seat loop, feeds itself, and B4, the accountability loop, pushes back. The loop works only where seats are competitive.

Overview

LoopR10 Reinforcing, feeds itself

Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates

In a safe seat, the primary decides who wins, and few people vote in it. With little threat in November, officeholders answer to that smaller electorate and face less pressure from the wider public. Officials who cannot easily be removed can then write election rules that keep seats safe.

Read it aloud More safe seats, more seats settled in the primary, less risk of losing office, more incumbents control election rules, and back to more safe seats.

Safe-seat loop. Four steps, each a numbered connection. One turn takes 2 to 10 years. Now running up: Share of House seats settled in primaries, 2012 to 2024.

Follow one change around the loop

Start at C1, Safe seats, and suppose it rises. Press Play, or Next step to follow one numbered link at a time.

  1. L08, Safe seats make the primary decisive. More safe seats means more seats settled in the primary. Plus, raises; documented; under 2 years. R-01 acts on this step.
  2. L25, Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure. More seats settled in the primary means less risk of losing office. Minus, lowers; well supported; under 2 years. R-01 acts on this step.
  3. L53, Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves. Less risk of losing office means more incumbents control election rules. Minus, lowers; plausible; 2 to 10 years. The weakest step.
  4. L42, Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats. More incumbents control election rules means more safe seats. Plus, raises; documented; 2 to 10 years.

In the model’s words

“Seats with little electoral competition raise how often the primary decides the winner, which lowers the risk of losing office; lower risk raises officeholders' control over election rules, which raises the number of seats with little electoral competition.”

What the evidence says

L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive and L42: Incumbent-drawn maps create safe seats are documented, and L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure is well supported. The weakest step is L53: Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves, graded plausible: its evidence is the 2025 mid-decade redistricting in states with one-party control and legal analysis. Whether primaries make legislators more extreme is a separate, contested question, and the strongest tests found no effect.

Keep in mind

Seat safety also comes from where voters live, and the claim that primary reform makes legislators more moderate is contested, so the loop concerns accountability more than ideology.

A plus sign means the two variables move the same way. It does not mean the change is good.

A real case

Alaska's top-four primary with ranked-choice general elections survived a 2024 repeal measure by 743 votes out of 321,203 after a December 2024 recount. As of October 15, 2026, a second repeal is on the November 3, 2026 ballot, combined with repeal of the state's rule requiring disclosure of the true source of political donations. One election cycle is too short to show the design's long-run effect on accountability.

Overview

ReformR-01 Rules · All-party primaries

All-party primaries with ranked general elections

Every voter, whatever their party, could vote in one first-round election, and two or more candidates would advance to a November ballot that all voters use. In seats that one party usually wins, the choice now made in a low-turnout party primary would move to the full electorate.

Disclosure

The Atlas takes no position on Question 3 or Ballot Measure 2.

Oath & Action's editor works with the Yes on 3 campaign for Massachusetts Question 3 and promotes it through Veterans for All Voters, where he is Massachusetts state lead. He also co-leads Ranked Choice Melrose, a local campaign.

The problem it answers

In a safe seat, the primary decides who wins, and few people vote in it. With little threat in November, officeholders answer to that smaller electorate and face less pressure from the wider public. Officials who cannot easily be removed can then write election rules that keep seats safe.

Open loop R10, step by step

What it changes

In a safe seat the general election is predictable, so the party primary picks the winner (L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive). That weakens the threat incumbents face from the wider public (L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure). An all-party primary sends more than one candidate to November, which aims to lower C2: How often the primary decides the winner and raise C3: Risk of losing office. A top-two design advances two candidates; a top-four design advances four and can be paired with a ranked-choice general election. The reform sits on loop R10 (Safe seats shift accountability to small primary electorates), loop B4 (Electoral consequences can improve public performance) and loop R11 (Party loyalty weakens consequences for breaking norms).

Routes to adoption

Four routes, from a state ballot to Congress

Who could adopt it, how open each route is for 2026 to 2030, and when the Atlas last checked.

RouteWho decidesFeasibilityNoteLast checked
State ballotVoters in initiative statesMediumAs of October 15, 2026, Massachusetts Question 3 and Alaska Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal Alaska's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election, are both on the November 3, 2026 ballot.October 15, 2026
State statuteLegislaturesLowLegislators elected under the current rules rarely change them.No check date in V7
LocalHome-rule cities, for municipal officesMediumThis route is closed to cities and counties in the 19 states that prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, as of October 15, 2026.October 15, 2026
Federal statuteCongress under the Elections ClauseVery lowNone in V7No check date in V7
  • High: The route is open, and the reform has been adopted somewhere through it since 2020.
  • Medium: The route is open in some places, and a credible campaign could carry the reform through it by 2030.
  • Low: The route exists, but it needs a coalition that does not exist now.
  • Very low: It needs a supermajority, a constitutional change or a reversal of court doctrine.

Source: Who Do They Answer To? Systems Atlas V7, snapshot October 15, 2026.

Who decides

States set nomination rules for state and federal offices. As of October 15, 2026, Where a state allows citizen initiatives, voters can change those rules at the ballot box, a route rated medium in feasibility for 2026 to 2030; Massachusetts Question 3 and Alaska's repeal measure are both on the November 3, 2026 ballot. Legislatures can act by statute, rated low because legislators elected under the current rules rarely change them. Home-rule cities can adopt the approach for municipal offices (medium) unless state law bans ranked ballots. Congress could act for federal races under the Elections Clause of the Constitution, which gets the lowest feasibility rating because most bills need 60 Senate votes while the filibuster stands (R-12).

What the law allows

States control primary rules within limits the Supreme Court has set. In Jones (2000) the Court barred blanket primaries that force parties to accept nominees chosen by all voters. In Washington State Grange (2008) it upheld a top-two primary that does not name party nominees. A ranked general election also requires a state with no ban on ranked ballots.

How it would be carried out

Supporters first draft a measure and qualify it for the ballot, or a legislature passes a bill. A campaign follows. Before the first election under the new rules, election offices teach voters how the ballot works. After two election cycles, results can be judged by turnout in the round that decides each seat and by the number of contested general elections.

What it costs

Implementation is a small one-time cost for state and county election offices. In Massachusetts, Question 3 would take effect January 1, 2028, leaving time to prepare. Party leaders and incumbents who are secure in their primaries lose influence, first as a threat and in practice at the next open seat.

Problem evidence

Plausible: some evidence

Cook Political Report rated 398 of 435 House seats safe for 2026, as reported by Unite America, an advocacy organization that funds primary-reform campaigns. Unite America's own count puts 383 seats (88%) as effectively decided in the 2026 primaries, which drew about 22.7 million voters, 9.4% of eligible voters. Both counts rest on ratings, which are forecasts, and on the group's definition of a safe seat.

Remedy evidence

Contested: evidence disputed

More contested general elections and more candidates entering races are plausible results. Whether legislators become more moderate is contested: a 2014 study of state legislators by McGhee and colleagues found that more open primaries had little consistent effect on ideology, and experimental work finds that primary effects depend on conditions. Main limitation: Alaska's top-four system has a short record, so there is no long-run U.S. test of a top-four primary paired with a ranked general election.

Tradeoffs

Parties lose control over who carries their label, and some voters lose a party ballot line they value. Ranked tabulation takes longer to count. When two candidates from the same party advance, voters from the other party have no nominee of their own in November.

How it could fail

Party organizations in both major parties and incumbents secure in their primaries are expected to resist. Parties can coordinate so that only one of their candidates competes; in Alaska in 2024 one candidate withdrew after the top-four primary, with party consultants citing the risk of splitting the vote. Voters or legislatures can reverse the rule, and nineteen states ban ranked-choice voting in some or all elections. The reform can also fall short if turnout stays low in the deciding round, or if voters misread the ballot and trust in results drops.

How to judge it

  • Share of seats with a competitive general election
  • Turnout in the round that decides each seat
  • Share of incumbents facing a credible general-election challenger
  • Voter understanding of the ballot, measured in exit surveys
  • Legislators' voting ideology, reported as exploratory because the best existing tests found no effect

Other ways to answer the same problem

Open partisan primaries let voters outside a party choose that party's ballot. Fusion voting (R-47) is another option, and proportional House districts (R-03) change the general election and leave the primary as it is. Two options are set aside as rejected. Blanket primaries are unconstitutional under Jones (2000). Turnout drives in closed-primary states raise participation and leave the rules on who may vote in a primary as they are.

Status

Where it stands, as of October 15, 2026

As of October 15, 2026, two measures on the November 3, 2026 ballot would change how primaries work. Alaska's Ballot Measure 2 (petition 24ESEG) would repeal the state's top-four primary and ranked-choice general election and return to party primaries. Massachusetts voters decide Question 3, which would replace party primaries for state and congressional offices with one primary listing every candidate, the top two advancing to November; if approved, it takes effect January 1, 2028. Nineteen states prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections, by the National Conference of State Legislatures' count.

The stance and the editor’s disclosure sit in the box at the top of this page.

Source: Who Do They Answer To? Systems Atlas V7, snapshot October 15, 2026.

More excess profits, more entry, more competitive pressure, and back to less excess profits.

No numbered steps: the missing chain is the weakest point · One turn: 2 to 10 years · Now disabled in concentrated sectors · 2 reforms aimed at it

Sketch: no complete numbered chain. Each step is drawn as a hollow line.

LoopR9 Reinforcing, feeds itself

Taking part in a successful repair may support the next one

People who help make a public decision, and then see it carried out, may gain confidence that working together succeeds.

More effective participation, more accountable delivery, more earned trust, and back to more effective participation.

No numbered steps: the missing chain is the weakest point · One turn: 2 to 10 years · Now a design target · 2 reforms aimed at it

Sketch: no complete numbered chain. Each step is drawn as a hollow line.

Overview

The shared language

Every line says what happens next, and how sure we are

Five rules carry every drawing in this atlas. Learn them once and every loop, chain and register row reads the same way.

1

The tip is the effect

An arrow runs from a cause to its effect. The word beside it says raises or lowers, and the tag on the line carries the sign. A plus sign means the two variables move the same way. It does not mean the change is good.

The tag points the way the step runs. A plus means the two move together; a minus means they move apart.

2

Texture is the evidence

Every connection carries a grade for how strong its evidence is, and the grade sets the line’s texture. Solid lines rest on the public record or strong research; broken lines mark weaker evidence. The register’s evidence bars fill each grade with its own texture, so the mix reads in gray as well as in color.

  • Documented: on the public record32 of 118 connectionsFor example, L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive
  • Well supported: strong research evidence37 of 118 connectionsFor example, L25: Decisive primaries reduce general-election pressure
  • Plausible: some evidence35 of 118 connectionsFor example, L53: Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves
  • Contested: evidence disputed7 of 118 connectionsFor example, L47: Hostile content may raise partisan hostility slightly
  • Hypothesis: untested7 of 118 connectionsFor example, T01: Competitive politics may sustain demand for local news
  • Conceptual: a step with no numbered connection3 sketched loopsB2, B3 and R9 are drawn this way.
  • Decides: an authority connection7 connectionsIt says who holds the power, carries no sign and never closes a loop.

3

Ticks count the wait

Small ticks just after the start of a line count how long the effect takes to arrive.

  • One tick: under 2 years38 connectionsFor example, L08: Safe seats make the primary decisive
  • Two ticks: 2 to 10 years45 connectionsFor example, L53: Officials safe from defeat write rules for themselves
  • Three ticks: over 10 years35 connectionsFor example, L03: Policy advantages add to wealth at the top

4

Loops have a character

Follow a loop around and count the minus signs. An even count, or none, makes it reinforcing: it feeds itself. An odd count makes it balancing: it pushes back. Eighteen of the 23 loops are reinforcing. “Improvement or decline can reinforce itself.”

LoopR8 Reinforcing, feeds itself

Housing scarcity strengthens owners' incentive to restrict building

When homes are scarce, the homes that exist sell for more, and owners' equity grows.

More housing scarcity, more homeowners' equity, and back to more housing scarcity.

No single weakest step: every step is well supported · One turn: over 10 years · Now running up · 1 reform aimed at it

LoopB4 Balancing, pushes back

Electoral consequences can improve public performance

Poor public performance raises the risk that incumbents lose.

More quality of public services, less risk of losing office, fewer incumbents defeated, and back to less quality of public services.

No single weakest step: every step is well supported · One turn: 2 to 10 years · Now running · 4 reforms aimed at it

5

Color is the layer

Few inks, each with one job. Labels and patterns carry every meaning as well, so a page printed in gray loses nothing.

  • Charcoal: The system: every variable, arrow and count, and the route a headline names.
  • Stone: Context: counts that run back, rules and hairlines.
  • Prussian: The fix layer: reform cards and the tab that names a reform where it acts.
  • Pillar Red: Where a reform acts, on the loop and reform pages only. One job per view, never on Prussian.
